newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil panel begins mulling telcom sell-off bill.
newsitem.headline: Brazil panel begins mulling telcom sell-off bill.

text.p: Brazil's plan to privatize its vast telecommunications industry moved forward Wednesday when a committee of the Chamber of Deputies met for a first time to begin mulling a bill outlining the sector's future.
Deputies in charge of the committee said they hoped to complete discussions and vote on the legislation by April.
The bill, which seeks to regulate the opening up of Brazil's telecommunications monopoly to private groups, would then move to the floor of the lower house. It also needs Senate approval.
The committee has been created to incorporate half a dozen lower house panels all of which would normally have to vote on the bill, and add months to its passage through Congress.
It will study and probably alter a draft copy of the General Telecommunications Law, drawn up by the Communications Ministry.

The law would merge state-level units of federal holding Telebras into regional blocks and then privatize them. It would also create a new sector regulator and fix regulations governing technical aspects of the industry.

Communications Minister Sergio Motta said last week he expected the sale of Telebras' regional units to raise between $25 billion and $30 billion. The government has not yet estimated the value of Telebras' long-distance carrier Embratel.
Deputy Paulo Bornhausen, elected as president of the committee, said the "spirit of the law is perfect, but there will be discussions about the model (of Telebras' privatization)."

Bornhausen, who is in his first term as a deputy and whose father Jorge is a force in the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL), will also be responsible for revising the parts of the government's draft bill that refer to privatization.
Veteran lawmaker and former transport minister Deputy Alberto Goldman will revise the bill's articles on the regulatory body and technical elements.
Goldman, a leading member of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), will have the final say on what version of the draft will be eventually put to a vote in the committee.

The government's decision to split the rewriting of the bill between Bornhausen and Goldman was widely seen as an attempt to appease the PFL and the PMDB, both of which are powerful allies of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
A second meeting of the committee was due to take place at 1000 local time/1300 GMT Thursday.
